title: Testing
summary: After this unit you can choose between unit tests, Spring test slices and @SpringBootTest, stub SuccessFactors with WireMock to test retries and timeouts, and explain where contract testing with Pact fits.
versionNotes: JUnit 6.1.3 (latest stable on 2026-10-25, released 7 August 2026). JUnit 6.0.0 (30 September 2025): Java 17 baseline, one version number for Platform, Jupiter and Vintage, JSpecify nullability annotations, Vintage engine deprecated, junit-platform-runner removed, Maven Surefire and Failsafe 3.0.0 or later. Unconfirmed: the Kotlin minimum (junit.org says Kotlin 2.1; the detailed 6.0.0 release notes say 2.2), so the unit does not state it.
Mockito 5.24.0 (latest on javadoc.io on 2026-10-25): inline mock maker by default since 5.0.0; on Java 21 or later the docs ask you to configure Mockito as a -javaagent.

Spring Boot 4.1.2 and Spring Framework 7.0.10 reference pages (checked 2026-10-25): @MockBean and @SpyBean were removed in Spring Boot 4.0; @WebMvcTest comes from the spring-boot-webmvc-test module; @RestClientTest is in org.springframework.boot.restclient.test.autoconfigure since 4.0.0; Spring Framework 7 requires JUnit 6 and deprecates its JUnit 4 support; @Retryable defaults are 3 retries and a 1-second delay.
WireMock 3.x documentation on wiremock.org (resetOnEachTest(false) and the LogNormal maxValue need 3.13.0 or later); wiremock-spring-boot 4.0.9; a WireMock 4 beta exists and was not used.
Testcontainers for Java 2.0.5 (PostgreSQLContainer is in the package org.testcontainers.postgresql).

Spring Cloud Contract: Spring blog post of 6 July 2026 says it will be removed from all future Spring Cloud release trains and continues as Stubborn.sh, led by Marcin Grzejszczak; stubborn.sh lists Stubborn Contract 0.2.0 under the sh.stubborn groupId, with the core under Apache 2.0. The last Spring Cloud Contract reference on docs.spring.io is 5.0.3.
SuccessFactors examples use the OData v2 path /odata/v2/JobApplication from SAP KBA 2882860; the SAP Help API reference pages could not be read automatically.
unconfirmed: whether the names of @MockitoBean fields are part of the Spring test context cache key, so the unit only says that a different set of mocks creates a new context.

unconfirmed: whether Spring Boot 4 changed how @SpringBootTest provides MockMvc (the 4.0 migration guide was not re-read in the review), so the unit only says that MockMvc in a @SpringBootTest needs @AutoConfigureMockMvc.

terms.def: The programming model and extension model for writing JUnit tests, with annotations such as @Test, @ParameterizedTest and @Nested. It runs on the JUnit Platform, which launches testing frameworks on the JVM.
terms.example: The team writes the tests for its SuccessFactors client in JUnit Jupiter 6 and runs them with Maven Surefire on Java 25.

terms.def: A Mockito object that stands in for a real collaborator in a test. You stub what it returns, and afterwards you verify how your code called it.
terms.example: A mock CandidateRepository returns one candidate, and the test verifies that the service saved the record exactly once.

terms.def: A Mockito mode, used by MockitoExtension, that reports stubs that the test never uses and calls whose arguments do not match the stubbing. It keeps tests clean; in the rare case where it reports a problem by mistake, you mark that stub with lenient().
terms.example: After a refactoring, the build reports an unnecessary stub, because the test still stubs a lookup method that the service no longer calls.

terms.def: A mock HTTP server for tests. It listens on a real port, matches requests by method, URL, headers and body, and returns stubbed responses, delays or faults.
terms.example: The test points the SuccessFactors client at WireMock and stubs GET /odata/v2/JobApplication to return two applications.

terms.def: A failure that a test produces on purpose, such as an empty response, garbage data or a reset connection, to check that the client handles it.
terms.example: WireMock returns Fault.CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER, and the test checks that the Cloud Run service logs the error and tries again.

terms.def: A simple state machine for stubs. A stub can require a scenario state and move the scenario to a new state, so the same request gets different responses over time.
terms.example: The first call to the OData API returns 503 and sets the state to Recovered, so the next call returns 200.

terms.def: A Spring Boot test that loads only one layer of the application. It limits the component scan and loads a small set of auto-configuration, for example @WebMvcTest or @RestClientTest.
terms.example: A @WebMvcTest loads only the application status controller, and the service behind it is a Mockito mock.

terms.def: A Spring Framework annotation that replaces a bean in the test's application context with a Mockito mock. In Spring Boot 4 it replaces @MockBean, which was removed.
terms.example: In the controller test, @MockitoBean puts a mock ApplicationService into the context, so no call reaches SuccessFactors.

terms.def: The Spring TestContext Framework keeps application contexts in a cache. Test classes with the same configuration reuse one context, so it loads only once.
terms.example: Two test classes mock different sets of services with @MockitoBean, so Spring builds a second context and the suite gets slower.

terms.def: A Java library that gives tests lightweight, throwaway instances of databases, browsers or anything else that can run in a Docker container.
terms.example: With @ServiceConnection on a PostgreSQLContainer, Spring Boot connects to a real PostgreSQL in the test without any URL properties.

terms.def: A way to test an integration point by checking each side in isolation against a shared contract. The consumer's tests generate the contract, and the provider verifies that it meets it.
terms.example: The onboarding service's tests produce a pact for the Candidate API, and the Candidate API build replays it before every release.

terms.def: A named precondition in a pact, such as 'candidate 42 exists'. The provider sets up this data before Pact replays the interaction.
terms.example: Before the replay, the Candidate API inserts candidate 42 into its test database for the state 'candidate 42 exists'.

terms.def: A Pact Broker command that checks whether an application version can be deployed safely into an environment, based on the contracts and verification results.
terms.example: The pipeline runs can-i-deploy for Candidate API version 23 with the target environment production, and stops if a consumer contract is not verified.

items.q: Your team moves a service's tests from JUnit 5 to JUnit 6. Which statement about JUnit 6 is correct?
options: It needs Java 17 or later, and the Platform, Jupiter and Vintage modules now share one version number.
It needs Java 21 or later, because it is built on virtual threads.
It removes the Vintage engine, so JUnit 4 tests can no longer run at all.
It replaces @Test with a new annotation, so every test class must be rewritten.
items.why: JUnit 6.0.0 set a Java 17 baseline and one version number for Platform, Jupiter and Vintage. Vintage is deprecated, not removed, and the Jupiter programming model with @Test stays the same.

items.statement: Since Mockito 5, you can mock a final class without extra Mockito configuration, because the inline mock maker is the default.
items.why: Since 5.0.0 the inline mock maker is the default, and it supports final classes and methods. On Java 21 or later, still add Mockito as a Java agent, or the JVM shows a warning.

items.statement: MockRestServiceServer sends real HTTP requests to a local port, so it is the best tool to test read timeouts and connection resets.
items.why: MockRestServiceServer plugs a custom request factory into the client and runs without a server. Spring recommends mock web servers such as WireMock for the transport layer and network conditions.

items.q: In Spring Boot 4, a @WebMvcTest needs a mock ApplicationService in the application context. Which annotation do you put on the field?
options: @MockBean, which still works in Spring Boot 4 but is deprecated
@Mock, which adds the mock to the application context
@MockitoSpyBean, which creates a full mock with no real behaviour
items.why: @MockitoBean replaces a bean in the context with a Mockito mock; Spring Boot 4 removed @MockBean. Plain @Mock does not register a bean, and @MockitoSpyBean wraps the real bean in a spy.

items.q: Match each tool with its job in the test suite of a Spring integration service.
pairs: Mockito
Replaces a Java collaborator in a fast unit test
WireMock
A real HTTP server that returns stubbed responses, delays and faults
Testcontainers
Starts a throwaway database or broker in a container
@WebMvcTest
Loads only the Spring MVC layer to test a controller
Pact
Checks that a consumer and a provider agree on requests and responses
@Timeout
Fails a test that runs longer than a given duration

items.q: Match each WireMock setting with the problem it simulates for your SuccessFactors client.
pairs: withFixedDelay(5000)
A slow API: the response arrives after five seconds
Fault.CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER
The server closes the connection, and the client sees a connection reset
Fault.EMPTY_RESPONSE
The server sends back a completely empty response
Fault.MALFORMED_RESPONSE_CHUNK
An OK status header, then garbage, then the connection closes
withChunkedDribbleDelay(5, 1000)
The body arrives in five chunks spread over one second

items.q: A Spring Boot service on Cloud Run reads job applications from the SuccessFactors OData API. You need a repeatable test that proves the client gives up after 2 seconds when the API is slow.

options.text: Start WireMock, stub GET /odata/v2/JobApplication with a 5-second fixed delay, set the client's read timeout to 2 seconds, and assert that the call fails.
options.why: WireMock answers over a real socket, so the HTTP client's own timeout code runs, and the delay is the same on every run.

options.text: Use MockRestServiceServer, because it is built into Spring and needs no extra library.
options.why: It replaces the request factory and opens no socket, so the read timeout never runs; Spring recommends a mock web server for network conditions.

options.text: Mock the RestClient with Mockito and make it throw a timeout exception.
options.why: This tests only how your code handles an exception you invented, not that the timeout is configured and really fires.

options.text: Call the SuccessFactors preview tenant and repeat the test until a slow response happens.
options.why: You cannot make a shared tenant slow on demand, so the test is neither repeatable nor fast.

items.q: Complete the test. SuccessFactors answers 503 once and then 200, and the client must try exactly twice in total. Note that the client adds a query string to the URL.
Put the steps of a WireMock test for a retry in order.
steps: Start WireMock on a random port, for example with @WireMockTest
Point the client's base URL at the WireMock server
Stub the first call to return 503 and move the scenario to a new state
Stub the call in the new state to return 200
Call the client method under test
Verify that WireMock received exactly two requests

items.q: An architect proposes Pact contract tests between your integration service and the SuccessFactors OData API, so that changes on the SAP side are caught early. What do you answer?

options.text: Pact needs the provider team to verify our pacts, and SAP will not do that. I would stub SuccessFactors with WireMock from recorded responses, and use Pact between our own services.
options.why: Pact is not a good fit when the team on the other side of the integration will not also use Pact.

options.text: Good idea: if the consumer test passes, we know that SAP's API matches our expectations.
options.why: The consumer test runs only against the Pact mock; without provider verification, nothing checks the real API.

options.text: Good idea: we can run the provider verification every night against the production tenant.
options.why: Verification needs provider states with test data, and replaying writes against production can change real records.

options.text: Drop contract tests and replace all integration tests with end-to-end tests against the preview tenant.
options.why: End-to-end tests on a shared tenant are slow and cannot produce faults or delays on demand.

items.q: Complete the Spring Boot 4 controller test. It loads only the Spring MVC layer for one controller, and the service behind the controller is a mock.
Every test in your Spring integration service uses @SpringBootTest. The suite takes 25 minutes, and most tests only check one controller's JSON, validation and status codes.

options.text: Move the controller tests to @WebMvcTest with the services as @MockitoBean, and keep a few @SpringBootTest tests for the full wiring.
options.why: A slice loads only the MVC layer, so it starts fast and fails for one clear reason.

options.text: Give each test class its own, different set of @MockitoBean mocks, so that every test is fully isolated.
options.why: Each different set of mocks is a different context configuration, so Spring loads more contexts and the suite gets slower.

options.text: Replace them with plain Mockito unit tests that call the controller methods directly.
options.why: This skips Spring MVC, so JSON mapping, validation and status codes are no longer tested.

options.text: Run the full suite only once a week, at night.
options.why: Developers then learn about failures days later, when the cause is hard to find.

items.q: Your @SpringBootTest classes declare a static @Container PostgreSQLContainer with @ServiceConnection. After you add a second test class with the same configuration, its tests fail with connection errors.

options.text: Declare the container as a @Bean with @ServiceConnection in a @TestConfiguration and import it, so Spring starts and stops it with the cached context.
options.why: The JUnit extension stops the container after the first class, but Spring reuses the cached context that still points to it.

options.text: Make the container field non-static, so that each test gets its own container.
options.why: Non-static containers are stopped after each test method, so the cached context loses its database even sooner.

options.text: Switch the tests to an in-memory database, so that no container is needed.
options.why: The tests then run on a different database engine, so PostgreSQL-specific behaviour is no longer tested.

options.text: Add a short sleep before each test, so the container has time to start.
options.why: The container is not slow to start; it has already been stopped while the cached context still uses it.

items.q: Complete the WireMock JSON mapping. It must match the path and check the query parameter separately, and it must answer after 5 seconds, so the test can prove that the 2-second read timeout fires.

items.text: For calls to SuccessFactors, I test against WireMock over real HTTP, so the timeouts, retries and error handling in the client actually run.

items.statement: If the consumer's Pact tests pass, the integration is proven to work, even before the provider runs verification.
items.why: The consumer test checks the requests only against the Pact mock provider. The contract is proven only when the provider replays the requests and its real responses match.

items.q: How do you test an integration with an external API such as SuccessFactors?
items.model: I use several layers. First, plain unit tests with JUnit and Mockito for the mapping and the business rules, because they are fast. Second, I test the HTTP client against WireMock, which is a real HTTP server on a random port. I stub the OData endpoints, for example GET /odata/v2/JobApplication, with responses that I recorded once from a preview tenant. This runs the real client code: URLs, query parameters, JSON mapping, status handling and timeouts. Third, I use WireMock faults and delays for the failure paths: a 503 followed by a 200 to check the retry, a delay longer than the read timeout, and a connection reset. Then I verify how many requests WireMock received. Finally, I keep a few smoke tests against the preview tenant, because stubs can drift from the real API. I do not use Pact with SAP, because SAP will not verify our contracts.

keypoints.text: Fast unit tests with Mockito for mapping and rules
WireMock as a real HTTP server with stubbed OData responses
Faults and delays to test retries and timeouts
Verify the number of requests
A few smoke tests against the preview tenant, because stubs can drift

items.q: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and a test slice, and when do you use each?
items.model: @SpringBootTest starts the whole application context, like production, but by default with a mock web environment and no real server. I can ask for a real server on a random port when I need real HTTP. I use it for a few tests that check the wiring end to end, for example the service with WireMock in place of SuccessFactors and a PostgreSQL container. A test slice loads only one layer. @WebMvcTest loads the Spring MVC infrastructure and the controllers, not the regular components, so I mock the services with @MockitoBean and test JSON, validation and status codes with MockMvcTester. @RestClientTest loads only the client beans that I name, which use RestClient.Builder or RestTemplateBuilder, and it gives me a MockRestServiceServer. Slices start faster and fail for one clear reason. I also keep the test configuration consistent, because Spring caches contexts, and every different set of mocks creates a new context and slows the suite down.

keypoints.text: @SpringBootTest loads the whole context, with a mock web environment by default
Use it for a few end-to-end wiring tests
A slice loads only one layer, such as @WebMvcTest or @RestClientTest
Mock the collaborators with @MockitoBean
Context caching: keep the configuration consistent

items.q: The interviewer asks: 'Why not just mock everything with Mockito?' Which answer is the strongest?

options.text: Mocks are great for business logic, but a mock of the HTTP client cannot show me timeouts, JSON mapping or status handling. For those I use WireMock or a Spring test slice.
options.why: It accepts the value of mocks and names exactly what they cannot test at the HTTP boundary.

options.text: Mockito is no longer recommended now that JUnit 6 is out.
options.why: This is wrong: Mockito 5 is current and integrates with JUnit Jupiter through mockito-junit-jupiter.

options.text: Mocks make the test suite slow, so I avoid them.
options.why: Mocks are fast; their risk is that they hide integration problems, not that they are slow.

options.text: I never use mocks; every test runs end to end against the real systems.
options.why: End-to-end tests alone are slow and fragile, and they cannot produce faults or delays on demand.

items.text: Pact fits between our own services. For a SaaS API like SuccessFactors, the vendor will not verify our pacts, so I use stubs built from recorded responses.

items.q: What is consumer-driven contract testing, and when would you not use it?
items.model: Contract testing checks an integration point by testing each side in isolation against a shared contract. In consumer-driven contract testing with Pact, the consumer team writes tests against a Pact mock provider. The test sends real requests, and Pact writes each interaction to a pact file, which we publish to a Pact Broker. Then the provider's build replays every request against the real provider and checks that each response contains at least what the consumer expects. Provider states set up the data that each interaction needs. Before a release, can-i-deploy asks the broker whether this version is safe to deploy to the target environment. I would not use it for public APIs with unknown consumers, for pass-through APIs, or when the other team will not run Pact, for example a SaaS vendor. It also does not test side effects or the provider's business logic.

keypoints.text: Each side is tested in isolation against a shared contract
The consumer test runs against a mock provider and writes a pact file
Provider verification replays the requests
The broker and can-i-deploy before a release
Not for public APIs, pass-through APIs or a provider that will not run Pact

items.statement: If the WireMock tests for your SuccessFactors client pass, you know that the client still works with the current SuccessFactors API.
items.why: WireMock returns only the responses that you recorded or wrote, so the tests keep passing when the real API changes. Add a few smoke tests against the preview tenant, and record the stubs again from time to time.

items.q: How would you test that your retry and timeout logic works?
items.model: I test it over real HTTP, because the timeout lives in the HTTP client, not in my business code. I start WireMock on a random port and point the client at it. For the retry, I use a WireMock scenario: the first request returns 503 and moves the scenario to a new state, and the next request returns 200. Then I verify that WireMock received exactly two requests, so I know the client retried once and did not loop. For the timeout, I add a fixed delay longer than the read timeout and check that the call fails. I also try a connection reset fault, because clients often handle it differently from an error status. If I use Spring's @Retryable, the default is three retries with a one-second delay, so in tests I configure a short delay to keep the suite fast. Finally, I put a JUnit @Timeout on the test itself, so a missing timeout fails the build instead of hanging it.

keypoints.text: Real HTTP with WireMock, not a mocked client
A scenario: 503 first, then 200
Verify the exact number of requests
A fixed delay longer than the read timeout
Faults such as a connection reset
A short retry delay and a JUnit timeout keep the suite fast

items.q: Your team is moving to JUnit 6 and Spring Boot 4. What changes in your tests?
items.model: Most Jupiter tests run unchanged, so it is an evolution, not a rewrite. JUnit 6 has a Java 17 baseline, and the Platform, Jupiter and Vintage modules now share one version number, which makes the build simpler. Some deprecated APIs were removed, for example MethodOrderer.Alphanumeric, and Maven Surefire must be version 3.0.0 or later. JUnit 4 tests can still run on the Vintage engine, but it is deprecated, so I plan to migrate them. Spring Framework 7 requires JUnit 6 and deprecates its JUnit 4 support, such as SpringRunner. In Spring Boot 4, @MockBean and @SpyBean are gone, so we use @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean. The test starters are now per technology, such as spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test, so I add the test starter for each technology that we use. Finally, on Java 21 or later, I configure Mockito as a Java agent in Surefire, so the JVM does not warn about dynamically loaded agents.

keypoints.text: Java 17 baseline and one version number
Vintage is deprecated: migrate the JUnit 4 tests
@MockBean is removed: use @MockitoBean
Test starters per technology
Mockito as a Java agent on Java 21 or later

points: 6.0.0 released on 30 September 2025; latest 6.1.3 (7 August 2026).
Java 17 baseline; Platform, Jupiter and Vintage share one version number.
Removed: junit-platform-runner, MethodOrderer.Alphanumeric, support for Surefire and Failsafe below 3.0.0.
Vintage still runs JUnit 4 tests but is deprecated: use it only while you migrate.
New in 6.0: JSpecify nullability annotations, FastCSV for @CsvSource, CancellationToken, --fail-fast in the ConsoleLauncher.
@Timeout fails a test that runs too long; the default unit is seconds.
Spring Framework 7 requires JUnit 6 and deprecates SpringRunner and its other JUnit 4 support.
Inline mock maker by default since 5.0.0: final classes and methods can be mocked.
Java 21 or later: add Mockito as a -javaagent in Surefire or Gradle, or the JVM prints a warning.
MockitoExtension (mockito-junit-jupiter) gives strict stubbing: unused stubs and argument mismatches are reported.
verify: times(1) is the default; never() is times(0).
Use ArgumentCaptor with verification, not with stubbing.
thenThrow(...).thenReturn(...): the first call fails, the next calls succeed.
Mock your own collaborators; do not mock the HTTP client to test timeouts.
A real HTTP server on a random port: @WireMockTest or WireMockExtension; reset before each test by default.
urlEqualTo and urlMatching include the query; urlPathEqualTo and urlPathMatching check only the path.
The most recently added matching stub wins; atPriority(1) is the highest; no match returns 404.
Delays: withFixedDelay(ms), lognormal or uniform random delays, withChunkedDribbleDelay(chunks, ms).
Faults: EMPTY_RESPONSE, MALFORMED_RESPONSE_CHUNK, RANDOM_DATA_THEN_CLOSE, CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER.
Scenarios: inScenario, whenScenarioStateIs(STARTED), willSetStateTo, for example 503 then 200.
verify(exactly(2), getRequestedFor(...)) checks the request journal.
Spring Boot: @EnableWireMock sets wiremock.server.baseUrl; record and playback saves stubs as JSON mappings.
Stubs can drift from the real API: keep a few smoke tests against the preview tenant and record again from time to time.
@SpringBootTest: the whole context; mock web environment by default; RANDOM_PORT for a real server.
MockMvc in a @SpringBootTest needs @AutoConfigureMockMvc on the test class.
@WebMvcTest: Spring MVC infrastructure and controllers only; regular @Component beans are not scanned.
@RestClientTest: only the client beans you name (they use RestClient.Builder or RestTemplateBuilder), plus a MockRestServiceServer.
MockRestServiceServer runs without a server; for timeouts and network faults, use WireMock.
@MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean replace @MockBean and @SpyBean, which Boot 4 removed.
Context caching: the same configuration reuses one context, so keep the same set of @MockitoBean mocks across test classes.
Boot 4 test starters per technology: spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test, spring-boot-starter-restclient-test.
Throwaway databases, brokers or other services in Docker containers for tests (Testcontainers for Java 2.0.5).
@Testcontainers with a static @Container field: stopped after the test class.
@ServiceConnection creates the connection details, for example JdbcConnectionDetails for a PostgreSQLContainer.
With cached Spring contexts, prefer containers as @Bean methods in an imported @TestConfiguration.
@DynamicPropertySource: a more verbose but more flexible alternative.
Each side of an integration is tested in isolation against a shared contract.
Pact: consumer test against a mock provider, pact file, Pact Broker, provider verification replays the requests.
Provider states set up the data that an interaction needs.
can-i-deploy before a release; record-deployment after it.
Not a good fit: public APIs, pass-through APIs, or a provider team that will not use Pact, such as a SaaS vendor.
Spring Cloud Contract: contracts generate tests for the producer and WireMock stubs for consumers.
On 6 July 2026 Spring announced that it leaves the Spring Cloud release trains; it continues as Stubborn Contract (stubborn.sh).
